comments.author: @walterlowe8322
comments.text:
I enjoyed this video. A few comments. 
1) At the 2:00 point you mention the saguaro cactus, which, BTW, is the Arizona State Flower. However, you pronounce it "suh-GWAIR-o." The correct pronunciation is "sah-WAH-ro". (ahh sound not "air". Some Arizonans do include the "g" and most Americans use the shwa sound, so it becomes su-GWAH-ro.
2) At the 2:22 point, while talking about the temperature extremes, you mention "the low elevation deserts," which are located in *southwest* Arizona, while simultaneously showing a picture of Monument Valley which is located in extreme *northeast* Arizona, with an average elevation of 5,200 - 5,500 ft.
3) At 3:25 you do pretty well with "Mogollon Rim." You pronounce it "moh-GOH-yown." The correct Spanish pronunciation is "moh-goh-YOWN." But, of course, you can't expect Americans to correctly pronounce anything Spanish. By agreement reached by the Arizona Broadcaster Association in about 1962 (specifically because my father, who owned a radio station covering the Rim country, lobbied for a decision) the broadcasters finally agreed to pronounce it "MUG-ee-yown." The "own" construct I used means "long o sound, like in the word own." Fun fact, Zane Grey didn't know how to say it, so he called it the "Tonto Rim."
4) at the 4:26 point you show Barringer Crater. Did you notice how close to the Visitor Center the meteor landed? Amazing! (Lame joke, I know.)
5) At 7:50 you talk about the London Bridge. I can't prove it, but Arizona legend holds that McCulloch thought the "London Bridge" he bought was the  "Tower Bridge" and didn't realize the mistake until it had been rebuilt at Havasu City.
6) At about 10:27 you start talking about Havasupai. I have hiked that mule trail three times, twice as a Boy Scout back in the '60s. On our 1968 hike, we were caught in by a flash flood. We scrambled up a rock face and found shelter about 10 feet above the trail. The water rose until it was lapping at our feet. I didn't realize, at that age, how much danger we were in! Later, my brother fell I'll on that trip and had to be taken out by mule.

I wish you had mentioned the skiing on Humphrey's Peak (Snow Bowl) and in the White Mountains (Apache Sunrise).

It says the odor of ponderosa's xylem oleoresin, detectable in sun-warmed bark crevices, usually resembles commercial turpentine; in the Pacific region it can sometimes smell like lemon rind. It specifically says vanilla/pineapple odor is characteristic of Jeffrey pine (Pinus jeffreyi), not ponderosa.
